utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. For the sake of the record, may we have the appearances, please? For the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, Kenneth Scott for the Prosecution and with me at counsel table of course are Mr. Vassily Poriouvaev and Roland Bos and Ms. Kimberly Fleming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. For the Defence of Mr. Vinko Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My co-counsel is Mr. Zelimir Par. I'm so sorry, I'm lawyer Branko Seric, member of the bar of Croatia. Defence counsel for Vinko Martinovic and with me is Mr. Zelimir Par, who is my co-counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. For the Defence of Mr. Naletilic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours, Kresimir Krsnik, Your Honours, lawyer from Zagreb, Christopher Meek, co-counsel and Nika Pinter, legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Are there any matters that the parties would like to address to this Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. If we could go to a private session for a few minutes? Because I would like to inform you about certain problems that the Defence has come across of late.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We will go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Now we are in the open session. In this case, we also would like to ask the Defence team for Mr. Vinko Martinovic to file us a new list of the witnesses. For those who have difficulty to come at this week, might come at a later stage. Is that agreeable, Mr. Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, our witnesses are here. We have a group here, we are still waiting for one, and then we shall have six witnesses here. They are the -- on the list that we have filed. I hope we shall comply with that particular sequence. We hope that the witnesses will be relatively short and that we should be able to finish this first group by the end of this week or perhaps in the very beginning of next week. So far we have no problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Today we will start the Defence case for Mr. Vinko Martinovic. We are expecting this case to be finished by the end of September, which means more or less one witness for one day. Yes, Mr. Seric, your opening statement, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President. We have split our opening statement in two parts. I will address the Chamber and my learned friend in turn, to present the case from the view point of Defence. With regard to the facts and general postulates of the indictment. And Mr. Par will then tackle the charges in the indictment themselves, in so far as that is possible, in view, and please do not be angry with me if I say what I have been repeating from the very beginning, in view of the general nature of the indictment. And the lack of specificity in it. My lady -- Your Honours, Mr. President, nothing is as it appears to be. Nothing is as simple as it can be, and vice versa. It is a question for all times. Is life simple and then a man complicated? Or is life complicated and a man sets out to simplify it? We are halfway through a case which speaks about war. What is war? Again, a question for all times. War is woven the history of civilisation, the history of man, and the history of man is unfortunately the history of warfare. We learned that in school. Unfortunately, all we learn is years when a particular war happened, regardless of whether there is a Punic wars, wars between Athens or Thebes or wars waged by Austria-Hungary or France or any other war. All we learn is years. Yet war is part and parcel of this planet. There is war between different species of both birds and four-legged animals. There is war for survival. There is war within one species waged for predomination, war for power. The drive for powers, is, Your Honours, a destructive driver. It is stronger than the sexual drive but it also can be stimulating. Yet war conceived by human mind and put through by human hands is the worst war of all, and it destroys all life. No rational being can justify war as such, but if you're attacked, you have the right to defend yourself. It is a natural right and a right in nature. It is a right between species and between humans who are one of those species. Both in relation to the community as such and in relation to an individual. I need to say something about self defence. In our specific case, I claim that the Croats acted in self defence. They therefore waged a just war. Their actions were sensible, necessary and proportional reaction to attack, as stipulated by Article 31(1) of the Statute of this Tribunal. The indictment sets out to paint a situation as black and white but as a -- there is nothing which is black and white, it was not so in Mostar either. Life is woven of colours. It is more real than film, and it needs to be presented here in the courtroom more realistic, as more real and more tangible than we would see it on film because that is the only way justice can be dispensed. Last year, speaking in front of a learned colleague, Fourmy, Mr. Scott agreed with me, I proposed that along side those Statutes and the Rules of Procedure and Evidence we all seemed to use as another basic document Shakespeare's comedy, Much Ado About Nothing. Not because there is anything funny in this tragedy but because the title reflects the situation and position of my client. He was not any special figure in this war. He never had any special powers or authority. He was just an ordinary man who joined the war literally from the street, and a few days later, in the middle of May, 1993, he became, through the concatenation of circumstances, a commander for a group of young men from the neighbourhood who called themselves "Mrmak," because Vinko Martinovic had a dog who was called that. Now, can you imagine, can you imagine, what serious unit it is with a dog's name? Yet they were serious combatants, they were combatants on the front line they guarded. They were 50 to 70 metres of front line throughout the war. And Vinko Martinovic together with them. And that was that. And a great deal of ado was raised about it. We shall prove, Your Honours, that this "ado," and I'm speaking in inverted commas, about him and about nothing, was created by the media. They wanted to fabricate, to manufacture, a culprit. For very many things that went on in Mostar, although he, to all intensive purposes, never made a step away from his defence line on Bulevar, and the witnesses will say so in the courtroom. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Vinko Martinovic was just a plain, ordinary foot soldier without any special role in the war, without any rank in the military hierarchy, with the lowest degree of responsibility, and limited action on the -- along the narrow line of the conflict. The only thing that he can be blamed for, and we shall prove it, Your Honours, was to pick up the rifle and go to fight, to defend his street, his neighbourhood, his home and his people. And how powerful was this farmer, as the ancient Roman said, is best proven by the reaction of Hans Koschnik, the international governor of Mostar. A month after his arrival, somebody wanted to take him to a very nice restaurants. I've been to it. I know it, which is called Stela, Stela, like a star, but he didn't understand that, and he said, "Stela, nix Stela," "Stela will kill me." And just as Hans Koschnik was duped by these fables, by these tall stories about the ill famed Stela, so did this Prosecutor's office also take over the accusations trumped up by Bosniak secret services, notably the AID, and unfortunately I cannot but say it, with the assistance of some Croatian secret services who presumably wanted to protect somebody else. And started persecuting Vinko Martinovic. In other words, the Prosecutor's Office took up the position of the Muslim side of the conflict and taking over, without reservation, witnesses served on them of questionable past and present, who had been subjected to the blackmail and undue influence of AID. And to conclude this part, Your Honours, the problem of Bosnia and Herzegovina, believe it or not, has always been insoluble, and we need to start from that. In Bosnia and Herzegovina and in the international community, and before this Court, we must start from the fact that in Bosnia-Herzegovina there are today three separate and specific political, cultural and religious entities which emerged in the course of history, who suffered man-made interventions from all sides and that includes interventions in the name of democracy, in the name of the international community, but which, however, more often than not proved to be a demonstration of force. One needs to understand, Your Honours, that they cannot and may not be outvoting, that they may -- that one may not and cannot speak in inverted commas on behalf of one side only. In Bosnia and Herzegovina, there are Bosniaks or Muslims, we shall allow them to call themselves as they please, and also Serbs and Croats. Isn't it natural that each one of them aspires to clearly define and bounded systems of their own. Bosnia-Herzegovina belongs to its citizens, that is true. But the reality is that they are of three flocks and the solution of the political question is a prerequisite for the economic, cultural, linguistic and other solutions. There are not all that many models, Your Honours. Bosnia-Herzegovina will either be a state in which all its citizens, across the width and breadth of this territory, will be sovereign or they will not be sovereign but in that case, cantonisation will have to be embarked upon in order not only to recognise the cultural and linguistic, particularity but also the territorial and political integrity. The international community seems to vacillate between these two options and the Prosecutor's Office seems to have a similar approach. Yet in some instances, it is radical, because what it means is an unconditional protection of the federation, which as we have seen has no federal units, and is therefore under a question mark as such. And witnesses who have testified so far and who will testify, who we shall hear in this case, have become hostile, allegedly now. I wonder hostile to whom. According to the Bosniak Muslim option, because they are victims, and automatically, their option, their political option, is the only right one. Your Honours, I believe that this case will shed full light on certain questions and that a formula will be devised for Bosnia-Herzegovina so that Bosnia-Herzegovina does not remain, and I'm paraphrasing now, a Croatian linguist, so that it doesn't remain Buridan's ass. With regard to the fact that the Defence is confronted with the indictment, and the facts given in the indictment, then we would start by saying what facts does this Defence agree with so that we don't have to prove them so as to make the work of this Honourable Chamber easier. It is correct that Croatia proclaimed its independence on the 25th of June, 1991. It is correct that the European Community recognised the Republic of Croatia on the 15th of January, 1992. It is correct that Bosnia-Herzegovina proclaimed its independence on the 3rd of March, 1992. It is correct that the European Community recognised the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 6th of April, 1992. It is correct that the Republic of Croatia recognised the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the 7th of April, 1992. It is correct that the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina became a member of the United Nations on the 22nd of May, 1992. It is also correct that on the 18th November, 1991, it was proclaimed that the HZ HB existed as a separate political, cultural, economic and territorial entity in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It is indisputable that on 18 November, 1991, the existence of the HZ HB was proclaimed. However, what is disputable is that it was supposed to be a separate political, cultural, economic and territorial entity in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina as is claimed in the indictment. The Defence has already proven by a number of documents that have been provided to it by the Prosecution, by witnesses, some of whom were testifying under a pseudonym but some of them testified as public witnesses, like Jozo Maric, Bozo Raic and also our expert witness, Davor Marijan and it will be confirmed. The Defence has submitted an annex, that is an analysed -- that is an indictment broken down, and I'm going to follow the facts that the Prosecution has established and I'm going to present the thesis of the Defence, the thesis that we are going to prove in our part of this case. The Prosecution claims that the purpose, the intent, of the HZ HB was to establish closer links with the Republic of Croatia. It is not correct, claims the Defence, that the purpose of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was to establish closer ties with the Republic of Croatia in the way claimed by the Prosecution. The intent is visible from the decision on the establishment dating 18 November, 1991. When the Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Yugoslav People's Army carried out violence against the Croatian people and the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina could not protect it because it had not prepared for the Defence, we know what Alija stated at the time, Croats organised themselves. They organised their units. And during the defence, they established Croatian communities as follows: Posavina, Herceg-Bosna, Central Bosnia, Usora and Vrhbosna. As the enemy attacks grew stronger, in the area of Herceg-Bosna, a need was felt to provide for the coordination of municipal units and to organise the defence of the centuries-long Croatian homes. For that purpose, the representatives of the Croatian people who were legally elected in the multi-party elections in 1990, members of the HDZ, at their session on 18 November, 1991, in Grude, made the aforementioned decision. The Prosecution claims that Croatian currency and the Croatian language were used in the HZ HB. In the HZ HB, Croatian money was indeed used, but we have proven and we will continue to prove, that it was used to a lesser extent than the German mark, and therefore, there could be no conclusion of the expansionist intentions of the Republic of Croatia in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Another issue is the language. The Croatian people have always used a Croatian language, which was also used by the Muslim people, which resided in the territory of Herzegovina. There was never such a thing as a Muslim or Bosniak language, and our Witnesses MB and Slobodan Praljak and Stiepo Andrijic, Jozo Maric and many others have testified to that effect. The Prosecution claims that the Republic of Croatia made it known that it supported the intentions and desires of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. The Prosecutor claims that the Republic of Croatia made it known that it supported the desires of the HZ HB. However, this is a very simplified statement which cannot be confirmed easily. The Prosecution exhibit P155 is a letter by Dr. Franjo Tudjman to Alija Izetbegovic and the date of that letter is 5 July, 1999. This letter confirms everything that the Defence of both Mladen Naletilic and Vinko Martinovic claim. The Prosecution furthermore claims that the Republic of Croatia granted dual citizenship to Bosnian Croats. This is correct. However, the Republic of Croatia gave Croatian citizenship as dual citizenship. It did not appropriate that part of the people. It did not just annex that people into the Croatian corpus in the Croatian state. The Prosecution claims that by the decision of 14 September, 1992, the constitutional court of Bosnia-Herzegovina proclaimed the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna illegal. It is correct that the constitutional court of Bosnia and Herzegovina proclaimed the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna illegal. However, the legitimacy, the authorities, and the power of the constitutional court is not only disputable but the Defence is also going to prove that the constitutional court via facta ceased to exist. It is enough to ask ourselves this: If the constitutional court proclaimed the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna illegal, how come that Alija Izetbegovic, the talked to, negotiated with and signed agreements reached with the representatives of something that is illegal, that does not in fact exist? We have documents that we have only received only recently, one or two days ago, and this documents are -- these documents are going to prove exactly what I have just said. Later on, the Prosecution claims that the international community has never recognised the self-proclaimed Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. The international community has never recognised the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, which was self-proclaimed on 28 August, 1993. What is actually correct? This is actually correct. But it doesn't mean a thing, because this recognition was never asked for, but if we wish to embark on theoretical discussions, then we can say that a state is determined by principal elements as can be found in World Book of Encyclopaedia, in 1990, and which says that the territory, population and sovereign government are -- these are the terms that determine a state, the term state generally means an area of land whose people are organised under a sovereign government. Many authors claim that for a state, it is not important that it should be recognised by other states. What is important is that it recognises the international laws and that it is subject to it. Therefore, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was an organisation of defensive nature which was established so as to help the Croats of Bosnia-Herzegovina to defend themselves from the JNA aggression and throughout all that time it was illegal. The documents and the organisation of the HZ HB and the HR HB and the HVO demonstrate that these were only temporary organisations which were needed during the war. Unlike the Serbs in Republika Srpska, which passed its own constitution and created a whole new system of laws, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna mostly applied those laws which were in effect in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. New laws and new regulations were passed only to fill the gaps and to adapt the laws of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina where it was necessary. In essence, the laws of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina were implemented and applied unless when there were valid reasons for their -- for those laws to be supplemented. The HZ HB and the HR HB advocated the sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina and tried to find a solution for all the three peoples trying to maintain the traditional status of Croats, the status of a constituent people. The HZ HB established its institutions as a necessity because of the collapse of the systems existing in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Presidency had stopped functioning irrespective of the things that we heard in this courtroom. This is not correct. The Defence claims, has proven and will continue to prove that the Presidency had stopped existing and functioning. The government ceased to exist. So the indispensable elements of the statehood of one state, and that is the government, the positions of the government and the implementation of power in the entire territory of a state, from the centre, for all practical purposes had ceased to exist. It is a rhetorical question, when we ask: Did the presidency and the government in Sarajevo have power in Banja Luka? They didn't. Did they have power in Pale? Did they have authority over Pale? No, they did not. And whoever says anything like that is lying. Were they controlling the situation in East Herzegovina? No, they did not. In other words, the agencies of authority in Sarajevo could neither communicate with the rest of the state, nor did they have any control over it. And we have already heard, Your Honours, from our expert witnesses that the banking system did not work, there was no border control, there were no customs, taxes were not paid, mail -- I mean it really sounds trivial reason but when you speak about authority, a government in an area but the fact is that there was no communication, that is mail was not delivered. Citizens trying to communicate with their family members in other towns, in Brcko, in Zenica, in Sanski Most, while living in Mostar, could not either call by telephone or send them a letter. So in order to have life in Herzegovina and in Bosnia, where Croats could have some say, where Croats could bring some contribution to have this life go on more or less normally, one will to set up institutions as a citizen's service. Likewise, one had to form the HVO in the first place as a form of defence against the Army of Republika Srpska and the JNA, and later on as an efficient and well organised military force with two components, military and civilian. It was a historical necessity and the logical corollary to the situation in which the Croats of Bosnia-Herzegovina found themselves in. We shall prove that. And it was logical that we -- that the Croats needed to do that. Mr. President, I do not know when you were planning to have a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, probably at 5.00. Then we will break for 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. We heard during this case so many things about the participation of the international community which was a necessity, which was necessary, which was indispensable, and had an impact on everything that was happening in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, and as a result of which we have today's situation, today we are in this courtroom and I am addressing you in my present role. If there hadn't been such a will, maybe we would never be here in this courtroom. What I'm saying is that it is absolutely certain that the international community could, at any moment, stop the war, but what I am claiming here is that it did have the power to do that, but the war as we know lasted for four years and it was only because the international community allowed it to last, either for its ignorance, stupidity, a decision, or for some other reason. These are not my words. These are the words of Adrian Hastings, a historian, a professor of modern theology and the history of religions of the University in Leeds. Operations in the Balkans would be extremely dangerous because one would have had to control an incredibly mountainous and inaccessible area of a large fortress against the enemy, whose strategy owed a lot more to Giap, the Northern Vietnamese general who participated in the Vietnam War than to a classical western military mission. Again, these are not my words. The estimate that one would have needed about 100.000 soldiers was said by Colonel McCaffrey [phoen], on 11 August, 1992, in front of the Congress board for armed forces, and such facts were -- sounded discouraging for the members of the board, who all witnessed and participated the war in Vietnam. Only a mere comparison with something like that was a discouragement for them. Paul Williams said, at a round table in Budapest, which took place between 25 and 27 September, 1998, before a war starts, two things have to be known. Firstly, there is no such a thing as international community. It is actually a seven-member group of countries which dictate the world and which are made of -- which is made of the United States of America, Russia, France, Great Britain, Germany, Italy Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. and the European Union. And secondly, according to Paul Williams, the strongest interests of that group are very selfish. They are not necessarily interested in preventing ethnic cleansing or genocide. They are primarily concerned with their own interests. The main interest of the United States was to preserve the status quo, to preserve the territorial integrity of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia. Germany had an economic interest because an influx of refugees would have been detrimental for it. The Great Britain wanted to preserve its status of a great power, by the historical ties between Serbia and Great Britain. The French wanted to maintain the balance of powers in Europe. Russia, who had their own worries, but they also wanted to preserve the image of a world power. The Chinese were playing up to the United States because of their trade relations and the situation in Tibet. That is why the international community wanted, at all costs, to maintain the conflict in its original area, within the borders of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, and prevent it from spreading on to Kosovo. However, as the conflicts intensified, the seven-member group of states, all of a sudden could not believe when it heard that in the former Yugoslavia, there were concentration camps and the first reaction of the American government was, "This is not true. This is not possible." The key, decisive role was played by the so-called CNN factor. When the reporter, Roy Guttman visited the Manjaca Camp on 19 July, 1992, that is the camp 25 kilometres south of Banja Luka, and when he published on the 2nd of August in Newsday, distributed in 800.000 copies, a photo on the front page with a title "a death camp in Bosnia," this started an avalanche. And there were some pieces of writing according to which it was estimated that there were about 30.000 Muslims and Croats in the camps only in the area of Banja Luka. As these scenes inevitably reminded the world of the Nazi final solution to the Jewish question, the general public and the humanitarian organisations got excited and they made pressure on the United States, which actually started sanctions against Belgrade. These were the words of professor Paul Williams from the round table discussion, "War in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina," which took place in Budapest in 1998. The Defence furthermore claims that the Article 3 of the document on the proclamation of the HZ HB, dating 18 November, 1991, proclaimed Mostar as the capital of that community. The selection of Mostar as the capital of the self-proclaimed Croatian community was ratified by a decree published by the President of the HZ HB on the 8th of April, 1990, by which he also established the Croatian Defence Council. The seat of the HVO was in Mostar. The election again was ratified by a decree issued on the 28 August, 1993, by which the HZ HB was renamed into the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. Throughout history, Mostar was considered the capital of Herzegovina and is the biggest town in the region. The area of Mostar municipality includes, amongst others, the following villages and neighbourhoods: Rastani, Bijelo Polje, Vojno, Potoci, Rudnik, Ilici, Djikovina, Panjevina, Rodoc, Podhum, Zahum, and Blagaj. Before the beginning of the conflict, Mostar municipality, according to the 1991 population census, had the following ethnic structure: Of its 126.628 inhabitants, 34.6 per cent, or 43.856 were Muslims; 33.9 per cent or 43.037 were Croats; 18.8 per cent or 23.846 were Serbs; 9.9 per cent or 12.768 were Yugoslavs; and 2.4 per cent or 3.121 were others. The Defence agrees with these figures and finds them indisputable. The Defence furthermore claims that the Croatian Defence Council already in October, 1992, was attacked -- Bosnian Muslims in the town of Prozor. It is not correct and we are going to prove that the HVO did not attack Muslims in Prozor. It was the other way around. However, one has to analyse everything that preceded the escalation of the conflicts between Muslims and Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Your Honours, we have heard, and we will hear, that the victory of the ethnically based parties at the first multi-party elections clearly said that the communism and the international Yugoslav spirit was a surrogate which had not killed nationalisms, or to be more precise, chauvinism. The Muslim Party of Democratic Action, the SDA, rallied around it, the majority of the Muslim population and its goal was to preserve Bosnia-Herzegovina as a separate political unity, irrespective of the facts whether it is going to be incorporated into some broader state creation and its other goal was to create ultimately a completely Islamic society. The Serbian Democratic Party, the SDS, which was the party of Bosnian Serbs, bore a -- had the same name as the party of Croat Serbs in Croatia but it carried more weight, because both in ideological and numerical terms, with regard to other two peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Both these Serbian parties in Croatia and in Bosnia and Herzegovina were part and parcel of a Serbian political movement whose centre was in Belgrade. Its goal can be reduced to a very well known statement about all the Serbs living in one state, which corroborates the fact that they did not recognise republican borders and that their main goal was to create ethnic borders. The party of Croats in Bosnia, the Croat Democratic Union, was called the same as the party in Croatia. In contrast with the leadership of the party in the period before the war, its voters made it quite clear that they were looking towards Zagreb and the Croatian president. The party advocated the decentralisation of government in Yugoslavia by transforming the country into a confederation in order -- so that the internal republican boundaries could be could be preserved and only if such a confederation could not come true, then separation from Yugoslavia would become the order of the day, providing for the equality of the three constituent peoples. The parties which won the elections organised the government, following the model of the lasting division, which the serious analysts at the time already found unnatural and incompatible with democratic practices and lacking functionality. And then the first time they entered the world historical stage the ethnic parties made it known that the views regarding the future of Bosnia-Herzegovina did not coincide, and this should not come as a surprise because the same held true over their interpretation of the past and the present. The war in Croatia in 1991-92, on Bosnian affected the Bosnian and Herzegovinian Croats in the same way as it affected those in the mother country. An attack Croatia was seen as an attack on Croats. As such, and that is also how the attackers were seen. Those were Serbs regardless of the republic they came from. Some of the Bosnian and Herzegovinian Croats voluntarily joined the war. The Bosnian and Herzegovinian Serbs on the other hand, joined the war in Croatia in large numbers because they considered themselves and their whole national body perceived as the guardians of Yugoslavia, the participation of Bosnian and Herzegovinian Muslims in the war, on the Serb side, was reduced to the activity of a part of the officers corps in the Yugoslav army, the recruits serving the regular military service and reservist organised in the Yugoslav People's Army. On the Croat side there were volunteers in the corps of the national guard of the Republic of Croatia, yet one would say that in either case, the percentage of those joining voluntarily was not too high and especially it was not equivalent to the role of Bosnia-Herzegovina as the beginning for the attacks of the JNA on Croatia. The area of Bosanska Krijina and East Herzegovina served as a support for attacks on West Slavonia. They also served as support on South Croatia from the mouth of the Neretva to Prevlaka. The commander of the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina even paid out Bosnian Herzegovinian reservists without the knowledge or approval of the presidency of the socialist republic as it was still called of Bosnia-Herzegovina, using for this funds of the republican staff of the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It is very important to note that at that time, the republican sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina was such that it will be much simpler to answer the question whether it existed at all. As I have already said, a part of the Bosnian Herzegovinian territory could not follow in the steps of the local population. And thus largely became an area of attacks on the Republic of Croatia. Apart from the use of the Bosnian and Herzegovinian territory, the Yugoslav People's Army also attacked the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina, as confirmed by the devastated by the destroyed Croat villages in East Herzegovina. The symbol of this victimisation, the biggest of them, the village of Ravno came to epitomise those sufferings and here we come across the first question: Is Bosnia and Herzegovina an aggressor in Croatia's eyes? Bosnia and Herzegovina is a theatre of operations from which the operative army of the Yugoslav People's Army is attacking Croatia and it is made of some of the local nationals who -- without the tongue in the cheek, embraced the policy of the centre in Belgrade, with the exception of the boundary areas inhabited by Croats and these are Posavina and west Herzegovina, with Livno and Tomislavgrad. The rest of the Bosnian and Herzegovinian boundary, deep in the rear, the war zone developed with at least two operational actions. The territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina thus played a highly unfavourable role for Croatia, with the extraordinary operational basis, which the JNA did not manage to put to proper strategic use. This fact again is attached little weight. The three constituent Bosnian Herzegovinian people had a very clear cut attitude to the war in Croatia. The Croats and the Serbs participated in it, whereas the Muslims endeavoured to remain aside in line with the well known Izetbegovic's statement, "This is not our war." If we perceive Bosnia-Herzegovina as an area which functioned in its territory as we know it today, and that is the period much time between 1878 to 1918 and from 1945 to 1991, then we can conclude that Bosnia-Herzegovina always survived, owing to special status it enjoyed. It is significant that this status, this guarantee of survival, that is indivisibility has always been outside the border of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In the Austro-Hungarian monarchy, it was under the ministries. In the socialist Yugoslavia, it lived off the balance between the Croat and the Serb question and towards the end of this state, it was actually joined by the Muslim question. In the late 1980s, this equilibrium, which until that time kept Bosnia-Herzegovina in one piece became upset and in late autumn of 1991 it ceased to exist. The Prosecution namely claims that then the conflict, the armed conflict ensued between the Croat Defence Council and the armed forces of the Army of Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which lasted until February, 1994. However, the war developments in 1992, already followed after a political foreplay in the latter half of 1991. Mr. Krsnik's -- that is Mr. Naletilic's Defence has already produced evidence to that effect and those were our joint witnesses. However, I need to say that politically speaking, that on the 24th of October, 1991, Bosnian Serbs founded the assembly of the Serb people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, on the basis of the plebiscite of the Serb people of the 9th and 10th October, 1991, on the 21st of October, Serb autonomous regions in Bosnia-Herzegovina were verified and confirmed. The next step was made on the 21st of December, 1991, when it was decided to embark on the establishment of the Republika Srpska of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that was put into effect on the 9th of January, 1992. This set in motion the separation of the central republican bodies of power in one part of Bosnia-Herzegovina and this process was brought to its close -- to its end. After the Serbs, the Croats of Bosnia-Herzegovina also demonstrated their need to organise themselves in a republic, which was less and less of a republic with every day. At a meeting of presidents of Crisis Staffs of the Herzegovina and Travnik regional communities in Grude on the 12th of November, 1991, it was decided that the Croat people in Bosnia-Herzegovina had to, at long last, start pursuing resolute elective policy which would and should bring about the realisation of our age-old dream about a joint Croat state. Whereas the conclusions of the meeting, spoke about the strategy of Bosnian Herzegovinian Croats and that was the establishment of a sovereign Croatia within its both ethnic and historical possible borders, six days later, there were denied by the decision on the establishment of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna, which stipulated that the community would respect the democratically elected government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as long as there was the state independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina in relation to another state or any other former Yugoslavia. In the decision on the sovereignty of the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina of the 15th of October, 1991, says among other things, that Bosnia-Herzegovina will develop as a civil republic and as a sovereign and indivisible state. It will be neutral in the conflicts between Serbia and Croatia, and it can remain in the Yugoslav community only if Serbia and Croatia also remain in it, and that is a reflection in point of fact of the Muslim option. For other peoples, that view was already obsolete, was already outdated. Yugoslavia was bursting at its seams and Bosnia-Herzegovina was a Yugoslavia in small. For Croats and for Serbs, Muslims were not adversaries but neither were they allies. And that was the situation until April 1992, when a new page of Bosnian Herzegovinian history started. The time before the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina was characteristic of the preparations of political parties for the war. The intensity of these preparations was not always the same. Basically, because the initial stages were different. The SDS was in the forefront. A Serb party which was supplied with weaponry by the JNA turned pro-Serb. The Croats also came by weapons through the HDZ, in significantly smaller quantities than the Serbs, but sufficient to gradually reduce the inferiority complex after the JNA had disarmed the republic and territorial defence. True, with Muslims, the situation was much less propitious, partly because they found themselves in the gap between the political leaders and the people, and nonetheless, they also started making some very early steps in that respect. The Muslim Patriotic League, which was set up on the 2nd of May, 1991, could be treated at that time only as a paramilitary party unit. After that, on the 10th of June, 1991, in the Sarajevo police house, at a meeting of leading Bosniak public figures, from all over Yugoslavia, was founded under the umbrella of the SDA, the Council of the National Defence of the Muslim People with the Patriotic League as its military wing. The political stage in Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time was remindful of the political scene in the kingdom of Yugoslavia from the time of the accord between Dragisa Cvetkovic and Vladtko Macek, when the political representatives of the Serbs and Croats solved the vital matters and the Muslims were somewhere in the wings. The common aspect of this so-called arms race was its -- was the ethnic principle which governed it. Everybody armed himself separately. At a military meeting of the Muslim Patriotic League in the village of Mehurici, near Travnik, held on the 7th and 8th February, 1992, it was concluded that they were available between 70 -- 60 and 70.000 armed members. Towards the end of February, the directive for the defensive sovereignty was adopted and it shows clearly that the Patriotic League considers as the destructive forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina the SDS with the Yugoslav Army and the extremist wing of the HDZ. The chief purpose of this directive was the protection of the Muslim people, the preservation of the integrity of Bosnia-Herzegovina, with a view to assuring once again the joint -- the coexistence of all peoples and national minorities in the state territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Item three of this directive calls on the people of Sandzak, Kosovo and Macedonia to give proof of their solidarity with our just struggle and engage immediately in combat operations and I'm talking about February, 1992, to immediately engage in combat operations, in order to tie up the enemy forces and weaken its striking power in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And the same time to establish contacts, cooperation and coordination in joint operations with the Croat people in Bosnia-Herzegovina against a common enemy. In relation to the beginning of the month, this was a major head way because the extremist wing of the HDZ is no longer mentioned. utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to continue, Your Honours, by saying that during 1991 and 1992, the JNA pulled out the troops and the material and technical equipment from Slovenia and Croatia, and from these areas, the JNA started a war in order to encircle, to round off the Serbian ethnic area. After the initial period, any success could have been achieved only painstakingly with a major engagement of troops and material and technical equipment. In the context of -- in this context, the significance of Croatian successes is strategically more important for a simple reason, it was tied to the successes of Croatia, which for both threatened peoples was the logistical base and support. We have to bear this in mind. Croatia was a logistical base and support. The defence activities and operations of the Croatian Army, or better say the national guard corps, on the borders with northern and, eastern borders of Eastern Bosnia-Herzegovina meant a direct support to the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina in depth, because by their combat operations they tied part of the Bosnian Serb troops and enabled, allowed for the logistical and humanitarian traffic. The Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina had least reasons for satisfaction. At the end of 1992, it had under its control the lowest ratio between their numbers and the areas that it controlled. The open Muslim Croatian conflict started with a foreplay much before the first conflicts in Mostar and culminated in the final break-up between the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the HVO. The Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina published a decree on the unification of the Bosnian Herzegovinian armed forces on the 9th of April, 1992. On the 15th of April, the HVO established its main staff, and there was also at the time a very Muslim nature of Izetbegovic's regime. The structure of that Bosnian regime, in which the SDA dominated and the HDZ was a subjugated partner, accelerated the break-up of the Bosnian state. Until January 1993, Sefer Halilovic accused Croatian politician its for the conflict between the Bosnian Army and the HVO. On 20 May, 1992, the HVO was officially considered an integral part of the BH Army and the agreement between Tudjman and Izetbegovic on the 21 July, recognised the HVO and the BH Army as separate components of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which will have a joint staff. The political breakup between the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina into two parts, being the HVO as the Croatian force and the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina as the party -- Army of the SDA under the more pronounced Muslim domination. The Vance Owen plan in 1993 was the last straw that broke the camel's back because the Croatian party perceived this plan as the plan that gave legitimacy to the power in the three provinces according to the -- which according to the plan were Croat, but in these provinces, the BH Army units refused to put themselves under the command of the HVO and started fighting. After the Trebevic Operation by which Alija Izetbegovic placed under his control the 9th Motorised and the 10th Mountain Brigade, and by after which he put the government under its control, the ideology of the Army of BH saw its final transformation, and the Bosnian Muslim element became evermore pronounced. The Islamic orientation of the army became stronger and Rusid Mominovic [phoen], the head of the Department for Religious Issues, in the administration for political issues of the BH Army claimed that as far as the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was concerned, the Islamic community wanted not only to cater to the needs of those people who believed in Islam but also that the Islam and the Muslim traditions became the foundations for the creation of the Bosniak Muslim state, especially if we wanted for the army to resemble its state. These units constituted a -- the foundation for the parallel system of command and the parallel chain of command used by Izetbegovic and his associate, Hasan Cengic. So that in April, 1994, the army administration for morale announced a research project under the title of the personal role of Alija Izetbegovic in the defence organisation of the people. On the 22 October, 1994, of the -- Alija was proclaimed the honorary commander of the extremist Islam -- Islamic fundamentalist 7th Muslim Brigade. The SDA forged the history of the country, so as to provide for the unitarian character of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Its ambition was to make Bosniaks not -- if not its main -- if not its only factor then at least its main factor. Bosnia and Herzegovina has to be an independent state made of three --

It is a reflection of profound mistrust and divergent views on the -- regarding the future of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is well illustrated by sentences voiced by one of the members of the War Presidency of Novi Travnik municipality. The fundamental problem of Novi Travnik, to authorities this is what this presidency member said. "The HVO and ours regular," as is said, "there is collision and conflicts take place and will continue to happen because the president of the government is not admitted into the municipal hall without an ID. It is better to split up rather than fight again. There were different offers to Muslims and Croats to set down -- their government." I'm still quoting this member of the presidency. "We have been trying to provide an equal number of people to the government on a parity basis." End of quote. The problem of dual authority is the crucial problem besetting Croat and Muslim relations in Central Bosnia, the area in which the war escalated. In his analysis of the causes of the conflict in Prozor, the commander of the operative zone of Northwest Herzegovina rightfully concluded that the only preventive measure that could put an end to such conflicts was the prohibition to have two commands, two armies, two logistic services. Along similar lines were thoughts expressed by the commander of the 17th Krajina Brigade of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, who thought that one of the reasons for the failed defence of Jajce was that one and the same town was defended by two commands. Unfortunately, this was a thwarted attempt to define the areas of responsibility and areas of jurisdiction which would have given both sides a very clear picture of where they were. The problem resulted from the conquer, from the territorial conquests by the Serbs and ethnic cleansing, because huge masses of expelled persons and refugees from those areas flowed into the area controlled by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the HVO, disrupting the ethnic structure and the balance between the members of two different groups, namely the majority of the expelled persons -- and Your Honours, we must be aware of that -- came from the rural environment and arrived in towns, into the urban environment, whilst bringing along, as their mental baggage, a completely different way of thinking, and it is not unimportant that towns, of course, had multi-cultural experience and the same would hold true of Mostar but that was not the case in villages. So that in Mostar, not only the ethnic, not only the demographic, but also the traditional, the customary, the balance in customs, was also disrupted. The Prosecution claims that on the 9th of May, 1993, Croat forces launched a major military offensive against the Bosniak Muslim population in the city of Mostar and the positions of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina in that town. After the negotiations in Geneva, the political and religious leadership of Bosniaks, Muslims, in Mostar, published the Mostar warning of the 5th of January, 1993, supporting Alija Izetbegovic and rejecting the idea of the confederation. The letter was signed by Zijad Demirovic on behalf of the SDA, Hadzisejdovic mufti efendi Smajkic and lawyer Faruk Cupina president of the Council of Muslims of Herzegovina. I'd like to add, in view of this question, the question of the conflict between the Croats and the Muslims, that modern theologist Hans Koschnik, who researches what is common to the world religions, has been emphasising for years that there is and can be no peace if it is not first established between religions and churches. This Prosecution affirms that during the period under consideration, that is the period of the indictment, the authorities of the Croat Defence Council introduced different forms of persecution of the Bosniak Muslim civilian population. From the point of view of the manner in which we shall present this case, and how we shall go about proving it, we need to say that the crime of persecution needs to be understood narrowly, and our client may be charged only in relation with other crimes falling under the jurisdiction of the International Tribunal. One needs to bear in mind the statute of the international military court and the international military tribunal for the far east, stipulating that the persecution must take place through the commission of other acts in the -- under the jurisdiction of these tribunals because everything is indicative of the view expressed in international customary law on this issue. Article 2, common to all the Geneva Conventions, says that this convention shall apply in case of a declared war or any other armed conflict which breaks out between two or more high contracting parties, even if one of them does not recognise the state of war, and if an armed conflict breaks out between two or more states, international humanitarian law will be applied automatically, irrespective of whether the war has been declared or not, and irrespective of whether the parties to the conflict recognise or do not recognise the existence of the state of war. The only prerequisite for the implementation of the international humanitarian law is the fact that there is an armed conflict. The armed conflict, as a definition appears also in Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions, regulating non-international armed conflicts, that is conflicts between governments and rebels and insurgent movements. In case of an armed conflict, conventions are not of much help because they do not provide us with a definition of its meaning. In practice, there are now and then some disagreements regarding the applicability of international humanitarian law to internal conflicts. The only criterion which should be applied should be the intensity of violence and the need to protect its victims. I'm referring to internal conflicts. The problems, however, arise when one of the parties to the conflict denies the application of international humanitarian law, even if the fighting goes on. For instance, it does happen that a state considers an area which is occupied as its own and leaves the question of the application of Geneva law open. In other cases, units of a state simply march into the territory of another state and appoint a new government. These puppet governments then proclaim that these foreign units have extended friendly assistance and acted with the government's consent, even though this government was formed only ex post. Is this then an intervention following an invitation or occupation? How is one to apply international humanitarian law? Through resolutions of the Security Council or should we have third countries bring pressure on it? All the provisions of the Geneva Conventions are contingent on two ideas, a combatant and a protected person but they are not mutually exclusive. So a combatant may become a protected person when he has been wounded, when he surrenders or becomes a prisoner of war, without, however, losing his combatant status. Additional Protocol 1 defines the notion, it is Article 3, members of the armed forces of the -- of a party to the conflict are combatants, combatants have the right to participate directly in hostilities. It is no coincidence, Your Honours, that I mention this in my opening statement because only combatants and combatants alone are allowed to participate in hostilities. A combatant is the only one who has the right to fight, who is entitled to use force or even kill, and he will not be held personally responsible for it, as he would be if he committed the same act as an ordinary citizen. However, a combatant nevertheless does not enjoy full freedom of action because of the means and methods he may use in waging a war are limited, are restricted by international law, and it is these restrictions which are the subject of international humanitarian law and especially the provisions relative in particular to the two warfare which are also known as The Hague law. A protected person is any person entitled to special protection. The Geneva law distinguishes between the wounded, sick, ship wrecked of the armed forces and then civilians, prisoners of war, civilian internees, civilians in the enemy territory and civilians in occupied areas. These notions only apply within the rules relative to international armed conflicts. In international armed conflicts, privilege status not Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. recognised to anyone participating in the hostilities nor is there any distinction between the categories of protected persons. It simply distinguishes between those who use force and those who do not use it or are no longer in a position to use it, such as the wounded, sick, prisoners, population who does not participate in the fighting. In order to draw the attention of the Honourable Court to what the Defence is trying to prove, and that is that in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and especially in Herzegovina, in Mostar, that is, there was no international armed conflict, I must point out the difference between an international armed conflict and a civil war. A simple definition of a civil war is that it is an armed conflict which takes place in the territory of one state, between the main party on the one hand and the rebel party on the other hand. It is the case of a breakdown of the system of government in a country, in a state, which leads to the fighting between different contestants in the fight for power. Article 2 of the Geneva Conventions from 1949 on non-international armed conflicts, and its additional Protocol number 2, Article 1 of the Geneva Conventions from the 8th of June, 1977, is applicable always when the conflict between the government and the rebels takes place by means of systemic hostilities and the use of armed force. This can be found in the commentary published under the general editors, by Jean Piquetet, 4th Convention, Article 3, pages 35 to 36. Protocol 2, additionally explains that internal tensions and conflicts, rebellions, isolated and sporadic acts of violence and other acts of similar natures, themselves do not represent armed conflicts, and therefore, cannot be subject to international humanitarian law. The international humanitarian law distinguishes between two types of civil wars: A non-international armed conflict of a high intensity, that is Article 3, and Protocol 2, and other internal conflicts which are subject exclusively to Article 3. If there is an internal conflict, there is no legal foundation for the application of the Geneva Conventions on the protection of war victims. This rule has already been applied in the Tadic case before this Tribunal. The key question is imposed here, and we are proving this in our case. It seems that the intention of the Prosecutor was to show that at the beginning of 1993, due to the operations of the HVO, a confrontation with the BH Army was inevitable. However, there is an intention, a visible intention, to equalise the HVO with the Army of Republika Srpska, and this would provide amnesty for the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is not corroborated by any facts. The Croatian Defence Council and the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina had some common traits. We have proven that, our witnesses have testified to that effect, and they will continue to testify to that effect. The 3rd Geneva Conventions, Article 3 -- 13, is about war, prisoners of wars. According to the 4th Geneva Convention and the Additional Protocol, civilians are all those who are not members of armed forces. They cannot participate in hostilities. The Prosecutor claims that the subunits of the Convicts Battalion attacked Bosnian Muslim population, civilian population, in the areas under the occupation of the HVO and the HV, and that they participated in the operations of the so-called ethnic cleansing. That the units -- subunits of the Convicts Battalion acted, either as part of the troops of the HVO and HV, or in the coordination -- in coordination with those armies. Wherever there were HV units on the Bulevar, and that Vinko Martinovic collaborated with them or coordinated his activities in the operations of ethnic cleansing, the Prosecution has not provided any evidence to that effect, and throughout the presentation of the Defence evidence, the Defence is going to prove that the -- the fact that the truth is contrary, Vinko Martinovic actively supported the nationalist ideas of Bosnian Croats. This is what the Defence claims, and very soon, you will hear that the Vinko Martinovic, are -- our witnesses protected. I would like to mention their names but I can't. The Prosecution also claims that throughout the relevant time, Vinko Martinovic had an effective and direct control over the members of his unit. The Defence refutes that allegation. Article 7 of the Statute says, "The person who has planned, ordered or committed or in any other way assisted or supported the planning, preparation or the perpetration of a crime mentioned in Articles 2 to 5 of this Statute is individually responsible for a crime." In Article -- in paragraph 3, it says, "The fact that some of the acts mentioned in Articles 2 to 5 of this Statute was committed by a subordinate person does not exculpate the superior of the criminal responsibilities if the superior knew or if there was the reason -- a reason for him to know that the subordinate person was prepared, getting ready to commit such a crime or that he has already committed them, and the superior has not undertaken the necessary and reasonable measures to prevent the perpetration of such a crime." It is clear that the purpose of Article 7 is to ascribe individual criminal responsibility at different levels. For crimes mentioned in Articles 2 to 5 of the statute. Article 7 implements the general principle of the criminal law that an individual is responsible for his crimes and for his acts and commissions. This Article prescribes that is an individual may be held responsible for a crime or for an omission to punish the crime committed by a subordinate person. Article 7, paragraph 3, of the Statute, lays down the principle which regulates the responsibility of the superiors, which is very often referred to as command responsibility. Some of the legal issues which rise in connection with Article 7 paragraph 1 and Article 7 paragraph 3 are considered in -- have been considered in other cases before this International Tribunal. This Trial Chamber, I assume, is not going to consider them again. One has to emphasise the different nature of criminal responsibility envisaged by Article 7 paragraph 1 and Article 7 paragraph 3, especially in connection with superiors, which is the most interesting point for this defence. Article 7, paragraph 1, is relative to the persons which are directly responsible for the planning, ordering, or commission or assisting and supporting in a crime. Article 7 paragraph 1 covers those persons who personally engage in illegal activities and superior who does not participate in the commission of the crime directly Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. but has ordered it or instigated such a crime. For example, a person who orders a killing of a civilian person can be considered responsible in accordance with Article 7 paragraph 1, as is the case with the political leader who plans the execution of certain civilians or a group of civilians and then puts a military commander to the commission of that crime. The criminal responsibility of such persons, be it a military or civilians, under such circumstances, is their personal, direct responsibility, and is the result of their immediate connection with the physical commission of the crime. It can be said that the criminal responsibility of the superior person for such concrete acts can be considered primarily responsible for the commission of such acts, which arises from the general principles of the responsibility of the participants. The general secretary in his report describes a command responsibility as it has been prescribed by Article 7 paragraph 3 of the Statute. I'm not going to quote because I believe that the Trial Chamber is familiar with this Article. Article 7 paragraph 1 says that the person who planned, instigated, ordered, committed or otherwise aided and abetted in the planning, preparation or execution of a crime shall be considered individually responsible for the crime. The principle that an individual can be held responsible for the planning, instigation, ordering, commission or abetting in the crime firmly is -- is firmly based on the international customary law. Article 7, paragraph 1, reflects the principle of the criminal law according to which the criminal responsibility is not ascribed only to those individuals who physically committed a crime but it can also be extended to those who in different ways participate or abet in the crime and in -- when this participation is sufficiently connected with the crime, in keeping with the principles of responsibility for being an accomplice in a crime. Different aspects of participation in a crime can be divided into the main participants and their collaborators. Therefore, the meaning of Article 7 paragraph 1 is to ensure that all those who participate directly in the commission of the crime or -- are held responsible.
